NPLify · P0 Technical Baseline

Reading the ERD — a guide to the six diagrams · v1.0

New XP Technologies Limited

8 October 2026 · Companion to the ERD & Data Model, Draft v5.2

Before you start

What this is. The ERD (Deliverable 1) is the precise description of NPLify's data: 54 tables and 4 views across six diagrams. It is written for engineers. This guide walks the same six diagrams in plain language, one chapter each: what the diagram is about, how to read it, every box in one line, the lines that matter, one story walked through it, and the things people get wrong. The diagrams are reproduced from the ERD unchanged; the explanations are generated from the same model data, so the two cannot drift apart.

Who it is for. Anyone at NPL or New XP who needs to understand how the system holds money and decisions without reading field lists — Operations, Finance, Management, and newcomers to the project.

How to read any of the diagrams

A boxOne table in the database. The name on top; each row below is a field: its type, its name, and PK (the row's own id) or FK (the id of a row in another table — this is how tables point at each other).
A grey box with just a nameA table drawn in full in another diagram and shown here only because something connects to it. The note above each diagram says where it lives.
A lineA relationship. The end with the crow's foot (three prongs) is the “many” side — the table that stores the other table's id. Read it as a sentence using the label on the line: “DEAL_GROUP has many DEALs (legs)”.
Solid vs dashedSolid (||--o{): the parent owns the child — create and delete go together. Dashed (||..o{): a reference, or a link that can point at several kinds of thing (a type column plus an id).
Dashed boxes with no fieldsDerived views — figures computed from the tables every time you ask (client balance, group entitlement, offsets, custody). Never stored.

The whole model on one page

Four domains, read in the order things happen. Configuration (Diagrams 1a and 1b) is set up once per client: who the client is, who may send and receive, and how each partner is used. Rates (Diagram 2) arrive every day: market snapshots and partner offers, versioned and never edited. Deal lifecycle (Diagrams 3a and 3b) is where money moves: an order, its legs, money in, the exchange, money out, and everything that can go wrong afterwards. Ledger & controls (Diagram 4) is where every movement is written down, and who is allowed to do what.

Five ideas that carry everything. (1) A project is a client; everything hangs off it. (2) Receivers live in groups — pots of entitlement; most projects have one. (3) A deal group is the order; a deal is one leg of it, with its prices frozen at quote. (4) A conversion is the one moment money changes from the client's to NPL's. (5) The ledger is written in pen: every balance is a sum over postings, nothing is ever edited.

Diagram 1a. PARTNER_CONFIG, PARTNER_PAIR, SETTLEMENT_REGISTRATION are defined in Diagram 1b.

1 · Diagram 1a — Configuration — project, parties and receiver groups

What it is about

This is the address book and the rulebook for one client. It answers: who is the client, who is allowed to pay money in, who may be paid, and under what settings. Everything in it is configuration — set up once, changed under approval, read by every deal.

How to read it

Start at PROJECT in the middle: the client and its settings. Everything with a line back to it belongs to that client. Then follow the two “who” chains. On the sending side, SENDER → SENDER_RECEIVER_ALLOW says who pays in and which groups they may pay. On the receiving side, RECEIVER_GROUP → RECEIVER → RECEIVING_ENTITY → RECEIVING_ENTITY_ACCOUNT is the four-level “address” of a payout: the pot, the party, its legal entity, the specific bank account or wallet. The grey boxes at the edge (PARTNER_CONFIG, PARTNER_PAIR, SETTLEMENT_REGISTRATION) are where Diagram 1b plugs in.

The boxes, one by one

BoxWhat it isWhy it is there
PROJECTthe client and its settingsEverything else hangs off it; a client with two unrelated flows would be two projects.
INTRODUCERwho referred the client; earns commissionOnly needed where NPL pays a referral commission.
RATE_SOURCEwhere market rates come fromEach source has a staleness limit; a snapshot older than that is not used for pricing.
SENDERwho pays money inThe person or company that pays money in. Not tied to a partner.
RECEIVER_GROUPa pot of entitlement; one default per projectThe unit entitlement is tracked on. Payouts within a group are ordinary; payouts across groups are offsets.
OWN_WALLETNPL’s own wallet (reroutes, pass-through)Only used under an approved reroute; the custody view keeps it honest.
THRESHOLDa limit that triggers an approvalAmounts, slots and rate variations that send an action to Finance or Management.
CURRENCY_PAIRa from → to currency pairCarries the quote direction, precision and the whole-unit rounding rule.
COLLECTION_SENDING_ENTITYthe account a sender pays from (provenance only)Provenance only — where a sender's funds came from. Never a payout destination.
SENDER_RECEIVER_ALLOWwho a sender is allowed to payRequired before a sender can be chosen on a deal; it also attributes collect-first deals.
RECEIVERwho gets paid: counterparty, sender_return or partner_transitThree kinds: a client counterparty (has a group), the sender's own refund destination, or a partner's endpoint used as the hop of a two-partner route (no group).
PAIR_RATE_SOURCEwhich rate source serves a pairA priority chain: if the first source is stale or down, the next is tried.
REFERRAL_RULEcommission terms for an introducerEither a percentage added to the sender share or a share of NPL's earnings.
RECEIVING_ENTITYthe legal entity behind a receiverA receiver may have several legal entities; each has its own accounts.
RECEIVING_ENTITY_ACCOUNTone bank account or wallet of a receiving entityBank account (bank reference + bank rail) or wallet (network + address + crypto rail). EUR via SWIFT and EUR via SEPA are two accounts.

The lines that matter

LineWhat it means
PROJECT → almost everythingThe project owns its settings, pairs, thresholds, senders, groups and partner configurations. Delete the project and all of it goes.
RECEIVER_GROUP → RECEIVER (counterparty only)A client counterparty always sits in exactly one group — the pot its money is tracked in. The other two receiver kinds (a sender's refund destination, a partner's transit endpoint) have no group: a payment to them is charged to the pot of the deal leg that pays them.
RECEIVER → RECEIVING_ENTITY → RECEIVING_ENTITY_ACCOUNTThree levels because they change at different speeds: the party you deal with rarely changes, its legal entities occasionally, its accounts often (and EUR via SEPA and EUR via SWIFT are two accounts).
SENDER → SENDER_RECEIVER_ALLOW → RECEIVER_GROUPThe allow-list: a sender may only pay the groups listed. It is also how a collect-first deal — money that arrives before any quote — is attributed to a pot.
CURRENCY_PAIR → PAIR_RATE_SOURCE → RATE_SOURCEWhich market source prices which pair, in priority order, so a stale feed falls through to the next one.

One story through the diagram

Setting up “Client 1”. Finance creates the project with its quote clocks (fresh for 5 minutes, valid for 60, 15 minutes of grace) and its policies (disburse to zero, bank fees carried forward). The default receiver group is created with it. One currency pair, USDT → EUR, priced from Kraken first and CoinMarketCap second. Two senders, Ayush and Naveen, each allowed to pay the default group. Two receivers, Sud and Raj — Sud with two legal entities (NewXP Entity, ReferScout Entity), each with a EUR account over SEPA; Raj with VoiceAIWrapper and a EUR account over SWIFT. Nothing here mentions a partner yet: the same set-up works whether Ali or Jeton does the converting.

Easy to get wrong

  • Receiver, receiving entity and account are three different things: the party you pay, its legal company, and the specific account money lands in.
  • A group is not a “type” of receiver; it is a pot of entitlement. Most projects have exactly one, the default.
  • A sender's return destination is a receiver too (kind sender_return) — that is how refunds go through the ordinary payout path with the partner's approval — but it belongs to no group.

Diagram 1b. PROJECT, CURRENCY_PAIR, SENDER, RECEIVING_ENTITY_ACCOUNT are defined in Diagram 1a.

2 · Diagram 1b — Configuration — partner configuration block

What it is about

One block per partner a client uses: how Ali, or Jeton, is used for this client. PARTNER is global and set up once; PARTNER_CONFIG is “that partner as used in this project”, and everything a deal needs from the partner hangs off it — prices, legal vehicles, the accounts money arrives in, the road and the name money goes out under, and which client accounts the partner has approved paying.

How to read it

Read it in two halves around PARTNER_CONFIG. The pricing half: PARTNER_PAIR (which pairs this partner handles and whether its rate hides its margin or states it) → FEE_STRUCTURE (NPL's fee for that pair, versioned) and FEE_OVERRIDE (a sender-specific fee). The money-movement half: on the way in, PARTNER_ENTITY (the partner's legal vehicle) owns the COLLECTION_RECEIVING_ENDPOINTs a sender pays into; on the way out, SETTLEMENT_SENDING_ENTITY (the name on the transfer), SETTLEMENT_RAIL (the bank that executes it) and SETTLEMENT_REGISTRATION (a client account the partner has approved paying). PARTNER_REBATE_RULE is the rebate the partner pays NPL.

The boxes, one by one

BoxWhat it isWhy it is there
PARTNERa conversion partner (global)Set up once; how a partner is used in a given project lives in PARTNER_CONFIG, not here.
PARTNER_CONFIGhow one partner is used in this project“Ali as used by Client 1”: fees, vehicles, endpoints, narratives, rails, approvals and rebate terms all hang off it.
PARTNER_PAIRa pair the partner handles, with its pricingWhich currency pairs this partner handles for this project, and whether its price includes its margin or states it separately.
PARTNER_ENTITYthe partner’s legal vehicle (name on paperwork)The name on the paperwork (PT-tour, PT Global Inc). Fixed on a deal leg at quote; only a reroute changes it.
COLLECTION_RECEIVING_ENDPOINTthe partner account or wallet money arrives inBank or wallet by kind; a bank endpoint cannot be used until its rail is known.
SETTLEMENT_SENDING_ENTITYthe sender name shown on an outgoing transferPurely the sender name the receiver's bank shows. Holds no money and no account details.
SETTLEMENT_RAILthe bank / EMI that executes a payoutThe road a payout travels, with the bank fee NPL expects on it. Holds no money.
SETTLEMENT_REGISTRATIONa destination account approved by the partnerA partner pays an account only once it has approved it; the registration is the partner's copy of the details, in the account's kind.
PARTNER_REBATE_RULErebate a partner pays NPLDrives the monthly partner-commission reconciliation.
FEE_STRUCTURENPL’s fee for a partner × pairVersioned: a new fee is a new row with a later effective date; deals keep the version they were priced on.
FEE_OVERRIDEa sender-specific fee on one pairReplaces the fee's total percentage for one sender on one pair.

The lines that matter

LineWhat it means
PARTNER_PAIR → FEE_STRUCTURENPL's fee is per partner × pair, so choosing the partner is part of pricing a deal; the structure is versioned and a deal keeps the version it was priced on.
PARTNER_ENTITY → COLLECTION_RECEIVING_ENDPOINTA bank account is always in some legal entity's name, so every endpoint — bank or wallet — belongs to a vehicle. The endpoint's kind decides which fields it needs; a bank endpoint cannot be used until its rail is known.
RECEIVING_ENTITY_ACCOUNT → SETTLEMENT_REGISTRATIONThe same client account is registered separately with each partner that may pay it; the registration carries the details as the partner holds them, in the account's kind (bank reference, or network and address). A quote cannot leave Inquiry until the entitled group has an approved registration with the chosen partner.
SETTLEMENT_SENDING_ENTITY and SETTLEMENT_RAIL → DISBURSEMENT (Diagram 3b)A payment run stamps the name it goes out under and the road it travels. Neither of these holds money or account details.

One story through the diagram

Ali for Client 1. Ali's rate includes its margin (disclosed-rate pricing), so PARTNER_PAIR USDT-EUR says so and the fee structure is NPL's 1.00 % — 0.40 % charged to the sender, 0.60 % to the receiver. Ali operates through two vehicles, PT-tour and PT Global Inc, each with a USDT wallet endpoint on TRC-20. Payouts leave through “Ali's EU bank / EMI” (expected bank fee 25 EUR) under the name “PT Global Inc”. Sud's two accounts and Raj's account are registered with Ali and approved, so any quote through Ali may proceed. Jeton has its own block: market + 0.50 % pricing, one vehicle, its own rail, its own registrations of the same three accounts.

Easy to get wrong

  • SETTLEMENT_SENDING_ENTITY is the from-label on an outgoing transfer, not the destination; the destination is the receiving entity's account via its registration.
  • “Collection” means money coming in (sender → partner); “settlement” means money going out (partner → receiver). Each direction has its own from and to records, and after v5.1 the two sides mirror each other: config → entity → endpoint, and group → receiver → entity → account.
  • The registration is the partner's view of a destination; the account row is NPL's. Keeping both is how a wrong wallet address is caught before paying.

Diagram 2. RATE_SOURCE, CURRENCY_PAIR are defined in Diagram 1a; PARTNER_PAIR in 1b; DEAL, CONVERSION, BALANCE_CONVERSION in 3a.

3 · Diagram 2 — Rates

What it is about

The prices. Three things are recorded: what the market said (a snapshot), what a partner offered (a version), and the day's comparison between them for each partner and pair. Nothing here is ever edited; a new price is a new row, and every deal, conversion and balance conversion stamps the exact rows it used.

How to read it

Left to right: RATE_SOURCE and CURRENCY_PAIR (from Diagram 1a) feed MARKET_RATE, a snapshot of one source for one pair at one moment. RATE_COMPARISON is one row per partner × pair × day; it is created by the first deal that needs it and reused by every deal that day. PARTNER_RATE_VERSION is one rate a partner gave during that day — a day can hold several. The grey boxes on the right (DEAL, CONVERSION, BALANCE_CONVERSION) are the consumers: each stamps the snapshot and the version it priced on.

The boxes, one by one

BoxWhat it isWhy it is there
MARKET_RATEa market-rate snapshotWhat the market said at one moment, from one source. Never edited.
RATE_COMPARISONthe day’s partner-vs-market comparisonOne per partner × pair × day, created by the first deal that needs it and reused all day.
PARTNER_RATE_VERSIONone rate a partner gave on a dayA day can hold several; a breached version freezes the pair until Finance decides.

The lines that matter

LineWhat it means
RATE_COMPARISON → PARTNER_RATE_VERSIONVersions belong to the day's comparison. A version is breached when its spread against the two-week average exceeds the pair's tolerance; quoting and conversion on that partner × pair freeze until Finance approves it with a reason, rejects it, or asks the partner for a better rate — which is simply another version.
MARKET_RATE and PARTNER_RATE_VERSION → DEALA quote-first leg stamps both at quote time. That stamp is the audit trail: six months later you can see exactly which market print and which partner offer a price was built on.
PARTNER_RATE_VERSION → CONVERSIONThe conversion names the exact version it executed at — which may be a later version than the quote's, and the difference is visible.

One story through the diagram

Monday 09:00, Ops quotes USDT → EUR through PT. The engine takes a Kraken snapshot (0.9000), finds no comparison row for PT × USDT-EUR × today and creates one, records PT's offered rate 0.8950 as version 1, checks the spread against the rolling average, and stamps the deal with the snapshot and the version. At 14:00 PT improves to 0.8930: that is version 2 of the same day; the morning deal still shows version 1, and a deal converted that afternoon shows version 2. Had version 2 been far off the average, the pair would have frozen and the afternoon deal would have waited for Finance.

Easy to get wrong

  • A market rate is a snapshot (one source, one moment); a partner rate is a version (one offer, one day, possibly one of several).
  • Rolling averages are built from confirmed versions only, so a rejected outlier does not poison the next day's check.

Diagram 3a. PROJECT, SENDER, RECEIVER_GROUP, OWN_WALLET, COLLECTION_SENDING_ENTITY, RECEIVER are defined in Diagram 1a; PARTNER_PAIR, PARTNER_ENTITY, FEE_STRUCTURE, PARTNER_CONFIG, COLLECTION_RECEIVING_ENDPOINT in 1b; MARKET_RATE, PARTNER_RATE_VERSION in 2; DISBURSEMENT_RETURN in 3b.

4 · Diagram 3a — Deal lifecycle — deal group, legs, collection, conversion, reroute, balance conversion

What it is about

The life story of one money transfer, first half: the money coming in and being exchanged. It covers the client's order, the legs that carry it out, the money arriving for a leg, the exchange that converts it, plan B when money is stuck, and the special case of exchanging money that is already held with no order behind it.

How to read it

Start at DEAL_GROUP — the order, what the client asked for (“get €10,000 to Spain”), one quote toward the client, one entitled group. Then DEAL — one leg of that order: one partner, one currency pair, one conversion. A plain deal is a group of one leg; a route that needs two partners (INR → USDT at Ali, then USDT → EUR at Jeton) is two legs, and the little arrow from DEAL to itself is leg 2 saying “my money comes from leg 1”. A refund is a return leg, funded by a payout that bounced (the arrow from DISBURSEMENT_RETURN). Then follow the leg to the right: COLLECTION is money actually arriving, in parts; CONVERSION is the exchange. REROUTE, SENDER_CREDIT and EARNINGS_RECEIVABLE are side records that hang off a leg. BALANCE_CONVERSION and ENTITLEMENT_REATTRIBUTION are the exchange-without-an-order case.

The boxes, one by one

BoxWhat it isWhy it is there
DEAL_GROUPthe client’s order: what was asked forOne row, one quote toward the client, one entitled group — even when the route needs two partners.
DEALone leg of the order: one partner, one pair, one conversionA leg carries its own partner, prices and state; a route is several legs; a refund is a return leg.
COLLECTIONmoney arriving for a forward leg, in partsEach part is verified separately; return legs and second legs have no collection — their money is already inside.
CONVERSIONthe currency exchange; NPL’s margin is taken hereExactly one owner (a leg or a balance conversion); the one moment money changes from client to company.
REROUTEplan B when funds are stuck at a partnerApproved contingency: through NPL's own wallet to an alternate partner, optionally netting dues the partner owes NPL.
SENDER_CREDITan overpayment NPL owes back to a senderAn overpayment or a refund waiting to be paid back.
EARNINGS_RECEIVABLENPL’s margin still resting at a partnerNPL's cut that a partner still holds; recovered on the partner's fee cycle or by netting on a reroute.
BALANCE_CONVERSIONexchange of a held balance, without a dealFinance requests, Management approves; it owns its own conversion and names the group it serves.
ENTITLEMENT_REATTRIBUTIONwhose entitlement a balance conversion movedMoves one group's entitlement from the old currency to the new one.

The lines that matter

LineWhat it means
The many lines into DEAL (PARTNER_PAIR, PARTNER_ENTITY, FEE_STRUCTURE, MARKET_RATE, PARTNER_RATE_VERSION)This is the receipt. At quote time the system photographs every choice and price and staples the copies to the leg. If the fee table changes next week, this deal still shows the fee it was actually quoted at. So DEAL looks busy, but it is just one hop plus its frozen receipt.
DEAL → COLLECTION (1..n parts, forward legs only)Senders pay in instalments. Each part records where it came from (the sender's account, as provenance) and which partner endpoint it landed in — which must be active, belong to the leg's partner vehicle and match the leg's collection method — and a user verifies it. Return legs and second legs have no collection: their money is already inside the system.
DEAL or BALANCE_CONVERSION → CONVERSION (one owner)A conversion belongs to exactly one of the two, never both. It is the single moment NPL's margin is captured and the money changes from client-owned to company-owned — the ledger (Diagram 4) hangs off it.
DEAL_GROUP → DEAL (receiver group inherited)The entitled group is set on the first forward leg; a second leg and a return leg inherit it. That is why a refund never moves money between pots.
BALANCE_CONVERSION → ENTITLEMENT_REATTRIBUTIONFlip 5,000 SGD of held balance into USDT to fund a payout: no sender, no collection. Finance requests, Management approves, and the reattribution writes down whose pot the flipped money belonged to.
DEAL → REROUTE → OWN_WALLETPlan B when a partner cannot take the volume: an approved route through NPL's own wallet to an alternate partner, time-boxed, optionally netting dues the alternate partner owes NPL.

One story through the diagram

The client orders €10,000 to Spain (DEAL_GROUP). It is quoted as one leg through PT, with the pair, vehicle, fee version and rates stamped on (DEAL). The sender pays in two parts into PT-tour's USDT wallet endpoint (COLLECTION × 2), each verified. PT converts; NPL's margin is captured and the client's EUR now sits at PT (CONVERSION). The story continues in Diagram 3b. If the payout later bounces, the bounce funds a return leg on the same order, attributed to the same group, which converts the money back and pays the sender's return receiver.

Easy to get wrong

  • A balance conversion is not a deal: there is no order, sender or collection behind it. It is NPL exchanging money the client already holds.
  • Legs carry copies of the order's client, sender and group on purpose — a leg must be priceable and attributable on its own.

Diagram 3b. PROJECT, RECEIVER, REFERRAL_RULE are defined in Diagram 1a; PARTNER_CONFIG, SETTLEMENT_SENDING_ENTITY, SETTLEMENT_RAIL, SETTLEMENT_REGISTRATION, PARTNER_REBATE_RULE in 1b; DEAL, BALANCE_CONVERSION in 3a.

5 · Diagram 3b — Disbursement, return, confirmation, fees, referrals and rebates

What it is about

The second half of the money's story: paying out, and everything that can happen afterwards. It is the payout machine (a run and its slips) plus its complaints department (confirmations, shortfalls, bounces, fee arguments) and the commission counters that tick per deal.

How to read it

Start at DISBURSEMENT: one payment run, draining one partner's holding through one SETTLEMENT_RAIL under one SETTLEMENT_SENDING_ENTITY. It owns DISBURSEMENT_LINEs — one envelope per destination, each pointing at an approved SETTLEMENT_REGISTRATION, the paid RECEIVER, and the DEAL leg it settles. Then what happens to a slip: CONFIRMATION (received, in full or short), SHORTFALL (the missing part, topped up next time), DISBURSEMENT_RETURN (the bank bounced it). BANK_FEE_EVENT is the fee true-up on a run. FEE_DECISION, REFERRAL_ACCRUAL and PARTNER_REBATE_ACCRUAL are the one-off rulings and the commission counters that hang off deals.

The boxes, one by one

BoxWhat it isWhy it is there
DISBURSEMENTone payment run out of one partner’s holdingOne run drains one partner's holding through one rail under one sender name, in whole units.
DISBURSEMENT_LINEone payment slip: who, how much, which accountPoints at an approved registration and at the leg it settles; a line to a group-less receiver must name its leg.
BANK_FEE_EVENTexpected vs actual bank fee on a runExpected versus actual fee, waived / carried forward / absorbed; also the bounce fee on a returned line.
DISBURSEMENT_RETURNa payment the bank bounced backThe money is back at the partner minus bank fees; it waits in balance or funds a return leg.
CONFIRMATIONthe receiver confirms a slip, in full or shortFull or short; short opens a shortfall.
SHORTFALLthe missing amount after a short confirmationTopped up with the next disbursement, funded from NPL's pool with Management approval.
FEE_DECISIONa one-off approved markup, waiver or overrideOne subject only — a return leg, a balance conversion or a payment run; standing rules stay in the fee structure.
REFERRAL_ACCRUALcommission earned by an introducer on one dealPaid out of NPL's earnings.
PARTNER_REBATE_ACCRUALrebate expected from a partner on one dealReconciled monthly against the partner's statement, usually received in crypto.

The lines that matter

LineWhat it means
DISBURSEMENT → DISBURSEMENT_LINEOne run, many slips, whole units only; the cents below one unit stay in the client's balance until they add up.
DEAL → DISBURSEMENT_LINE (deal_id)Each slip names the leg it settles. For a client counterparty the pot comes from the receiver's group; for a refund or transit receiver — which has no group — the pot is the group of the leg named here. This is what makes “whose pot did this payment reduce?” answerable for every slip (ERD D17).
RECEIVER → DISBURSEMENT_LINE (paid receiver)If a counterparty is paid from a leg attributed to a different group, that is an offset: Management approval and tighter aging. A refund or transit payout is never an offset.
DISBURSEMENT_LINE → DISBURSEMENT_RETURN → DEAL (Diagram 3a)The bridge between the two diagrams. A bounced slip's money is back at the partner minus bank fees; it either waits in balance or funds a return leg, and the story runs again in reverse.
CONFIRMATION → SHORTFALL ← DISBURSEMENT (topped up by)A short confirmation opens a shortfall; a later run tops it up, funded from NPL's pool with Management approval.
DEAL / BALANCE_CONVERSION / DISBURSEMENT ⇢ FEE_DECISION (dashed)A polymorphic link: the decision's subject can be any of the three. A one-off, approved markup, waiver or override — the standing rules stay in the fee structure.

One story through the diagram

A run drains PT's EUR holding through “Ali's EU bank” under the name “PT Global Inc” (DISBURSEMENT): three slips to three approved accounts, each naming its deal leg (DISBURSEMENT_LINE). Two are confirmed in full (CONFIRMATION); one arrives €50 short because the bank took a fee — a SHORTFALL opens and the next run tops it up. A fourth slip bounces (DISBURSEMENT_RETURN): the money is back at PT minus €15, the bounce fee is booked (BANK_FEE_EVENT), and the bounce funds a return leg back in Diagram 3a. Meanwhile the introducer's commission and the rebate Jeton owes accrue on each deal.

Easy to get wrong

  • A shortfall is money the receiver is still owed; a return is money that came back. Different records, different fixes.
  • An offset is not a ledger event — the postings are ordinary; what changes is the entitlement view.

Diagram 4. OWN_WALLET, RECEIVER, SENDER, INTRODUCER are defined in Diagram 1a; PARTNER_CONFIG in 1b; COLLECTION, CONVERSION, BALANCE_CONVERSION, REROUTE in 3a; DISBURSEMENT, DISBURSEMENT_RETURN, CONFIRMATION, BANK_FEE_EVENT, REFERRAL_ACCRUAL, PARTNER_REBATE_ACCRUAL in 3b.

6 · Diagram 4 — Ledger & controls

What it is about

The notebook at the back of the shop where every coin that moves is written down — plus the grown-ups who are allowed to write in it. Every money movement from Diagrams 3a and 3b arrives here as one balanced transaction; every balance anyone sees anywhere is a sum over these lines.

How to read it

Three boxes carry the money. LEDGER_ACCOUNT is a jar with a four-word label — OWNER.HOLDER.CURRENCY.PURPOSE: whose money (CL = the client's, CO = the company's), where it is (a partner, NPL's own wallet, the project), the currency, and what it is for (collected, due, in transit, held, payable, pool…). LEDGER_TRANSACTION is one move, stapled to the event that caused it (the grey boxes along the top: a collection, a conversion, a disbursement…). LEDGER_POSTING is one scribble in that move — a debit or credit on one jar — tagged with whose money it is and what kind of cost it is. The four boxes on the right are the controls: USER, APPROVAL, AUDIT_LOG, RECORD_LOCK.

The boxes, one by one

BoxWhat it isWhy it is there
LEDGER_TRANSACTIONone balanced money move, caused by one eventAppend-only; a correction is a new transaction that names the one it reverses.
LEDGER_POSTINGone debit or credit line of a transactionIts lines add to zero per currency; each carries whose money it is and what kind of cost it is.
LEDGER_ACCOUNTa jar of money: OWNER.HOLDER.CCY.PURPOSEOwner (client or company), where the money is, the currency, and what it is for.
USERa staff member and their roleOperations, Finance or Management; Operations never sees derived economics.
APPROVALa request approved by a different personRequested, approved, rejected or escalated; the approver is never the requester.
AUDIT_LOGwho changed which field, whenField-level history of every change, with the acting user.
RECORD_LOCKsomeone is editing this recordPrevents two people editing the same record at once.

The lines that matter

LineWhat it means
The grey boxes ⇢ LEDGER_TRANSACTION (dashed)Every transaction has a receipt: source_type and source_id say which collection, conversion, disbursement, return, confirmation, fee event, reroute, referral or rebate caused it. Nothing is ever written “just because”.
LEDGER_TRANSACTION → LEDGER_POSTING → LEDGER_ACCOUNTMoney never appears or vanishes; it only moves from jar to jar, so a move is at least two scribbles that cancel — and they cancel per currency, because you cannot add apples to oranges. A conversion has a USDT half and a EUR half that each balance on their own.
LEDGER_TRANSACTION → itself (reversal_of_id)Written in pen, never erased. A mistake is fixed by a new transaction that says “this undoes that one”; both stay visible forever.
PARTNER_CONFIG, OWN_WALLET, RECEIVER, SENDER, INTRODUCER ⇢ LEDGER_ACCOUNT (holder)A jar's holder is whoever actually holds the money; a settlement rail or a narrative never does, so neither is ever a holder.
USER → LEDGER_TRANSACTION, APPROVAL, AUDIT_LOGWho posted it, who asked and who approved (never the same person), and who changed which field when.

One story through the diagram

A sender pays 1,000 USDT. (1) It arrives: +1,000 in the client's “USDT at PT, collected” jar and +1,000 in “we owe the client's receivers USDT” — the two shelves (where it is / who we owe) agree. (2) PT converts it: the USDT half takes 1,000 off both USDT jars; the EUR half puts, say, 890 into the client's EUR jars and 10 into NPL's pool — the only moment any money changes colour from client to company. (3) PT pays the receiver: −890 from the client's EUR-at-PT jar and −890 from the EUR payable; both shelves are back to zero. (4) It bounces: +885 back into the client's EUR jars, and the €5 bank fee lands in whichever expense jar the fee decision says. At no point did anyone “edit a balance”; every number on the shelf is the sum of its scribbles.

Easy to get wrong

  • Almost none of the money in the system belongs to NPL. Most jars are CL jars; money changes to CO at exactly one event — margin recognition at conversion. NPL never advances money to a receiver.
  • Client money is written on two mirrored shelves — assets that say where it is, liabilities that say to whom it is owed — and they must always add up to the same number per currency. Group entitlement is a view on the payable, not a jar.
  • The dashed boxes (CLIENT_BALANCE, GROUP_ENTITLEMENT, OFFSET, CUSTODY) are calculators, not tables: counted again every time you ask, so they can never disagree with the notebook.

7 · One deal, all six diagrams

Ayush, a sender of Client 1, wants to pay Raj €2,000-worth of USDT.

  1. Configuration (1a, 1b). Ayush is a SENDER allowed to pay the default group; Raj is a counterparty RECEIVER in it, with VoiceAIWrapper as his entity and a EUR account over SWIFT. Ali's block for this client says: USDT → EUR, disclosed-rate pricing, NPL fee 1.00 % (0.40 / 0.60), vehicles PT-tour and PT Global with USDT wallets, payouts through “Ali's EU bank” under “PT Global Inc”, and Raj's account approved by Ali.
  2. Rates (2). Ops quotes: a Kraken snapshot is taken, today's PT × USDT-EUR comparison is created or reused, PT's offered rate is recorded as a version and checked for a breach; the deal stamps both.
  3. Deal, money in (3a). One DEAL_GROUP, one forward DEAL leg with the receipt stapled on. Ayush pays into PT-tour's USDT wallet endpoint — the endpoint is active, belongs to the vehicle on the leg and is a wallet because the leg collects crypto — and Ops verifies the COLLECTION. PT converts; NPL's 0.60 % receiver fee and margin are captured in the CONVERSION.
  4. Money out (3b). A DISBURSEMENT drains PT's EUR through the rail under the narrative; one DISBURSEMENT_LINE to Raj's registered account, naming the leg it settles. Raj's bank confirms in full (CONFIRMATION); the expected 25 EUR bank fee is trued up (BANK_FEE_EVENT).
  5. Ledger (4). Four balanced transactions were written along the way — collection, conversion, disbursement, confirmation — each stapled to its source, each line tagged client or company and principal, earnings or bank fee. Finance's daily identity holds: client money at partners equals what is owed to the client's receivers, and the default group's entitlement equals the client balance.

Guide v1.0 — companion to ERD Draft v5.2. Names, amounts and rates in the stories are illustrative.
